What's something that your parents did that you only truly appreciated/understood when you became and adult?
Had children. Never occurred to me that I wouldn't be here if it want for them until I got older. Took me a while to get on board with that existential thought thing...
Being careful with your possessions. Some things in life are fucking expensive.

And proper consequences if you broke your shit. So many kid friends I had got new stuff if the broke it. My parents were not poor, but if I broke something from carelessness, I wouldn't get a new one. If I thought that was unfair, I would have to describe how it broke. If it was genuinely not my fault, then they'd get a new one. Other wise, I just got cold indifference, and I'm glad for it.

I do struggle with this currently. On one hand, I can just give my child what they want and be done with it. On the other hand I can teach them a lesson that will last forever. It's a difficult balance trying to be nice to your children, to give them things you want them to have, but also to not spoil them and have them assume things are handed to them.

I dont think thats necessary to not buy them a replacement. I mean it takes a week or so to replace it so its not like they feel the pain. And kids should have empathy for their parents and so you only need to explain that its a pain for you to buy again.
Buying me books, Parents weren't rich but my mum always bought me books which instilled a healthy habit of reading/researching things.
I grew up extremely poor, but books were always my treats. If I did well on a test or sporting event, I'd get a new novel. It has had a huge impact on my life, interests, and who I am as a person.
Yeah it makes up for the fact my parents couldn't afford the latest buzz lightyear toy etc when everyone else had one, looking back I know which i would rather have had.

Not giving me an allowance. I was always jealous because my friends got money every week but I only got money from Christmas and birthday. Now that I'm older I appreciate it though as I am more careful with my money and work harder to earn it. I look at my friends that had allowances and most of them are spoiled or bad with money.

But you can teach that lesson even better by giving kids an allowance, but making them earn it.

I got an allowance each week if I did all my chores. Taught me that money had to be earned, and taught me the value of it. I learned quick that the cash represented hours of work.

Knowing what had to be done to earn it ment that I was careful how I spent it since I knew that mowing the lawn and doing the dishes/cleaning all week was a waste if I just blew the rewards on candy.

My Dad grew up in Virginia. Loved baseball. His favorite memories were catching a Washington Senators game with his Dad. Of endless hours throwing the ball around and playing baseball with his friends.

He took a job in Buffalo. When I was young, hockey came to town. The first sporting event I ever saw live was a Sabres game. I loved hockey...and I hated baseball.

My Dad dreamed of playing catch with his son. One of my earliest memories is of him teaching me hot to hold a bat. He took a job coaching the local kids, in anticipation for the day when his sons would play. The hardest thing I ever did as a kid was tell my Dad that I wanted to play hockey again.

Here's the thing that impressed me with what it means to be a Father. He never made me feel bad for my decision. Instead he found a way (which, I have no idea how...we were broke) to sign me up to play. Even though he hated the cold, and had never seen a hockey game before taking me, he learned the game. When our hockey coach died, and our team had nobody to take over, he taught himself how to ice skate so he could take over coaching that year.

It's what Father's do. We set aside our hopes and dreams so that our children can follow theirs.

As I became an adult, I thought about my Dad when my son said he didn't want to play hockey, and he would rather take Tae Kwon Do lessons. I stopped thinking about him being another kid from South Buffalo to hold the cup over his head. Instead I took him to classes for years. I signed up for classes myself so I would understand what he was doing. I've watched him become a black belt, and the sense of pride he has in his accomplishment.

I don't think I would have been as good a father a I am if not for watching what my Dad did for me.

My dad gets up for work at 4:45am, leaves by 6, and gets home after 7pm, 5 days a week. He usually works from home on Saturdays too. He's been doing this for 30+ years. My siblings and I were much closer to our mom because she was the one who was always around. Now looking back, I respect my dad so much for how hard he works. His work ethic is the best I know. I don't know what my future holds but I hope I learn to be as responsible as he is.
if at all possible never miss work, your boss will appreciate you being there everyday

They made decisions as a team and put up a unified front. I always thought it meant they agreed on everything, but now that I'm an adult, I've talked to them about some of those decisions and realized that they had different views and constantly argued about what to do. It was smart to keep those arguments private so I wouldn't blame one of them or play them against each other to get my way. On the other hand, it's amazing to me that some of the things they decided were so one-sided when I thought they agreed completely.

Actually, now that I have kids of my own, I really understand how precious their time with me was, and still is. The first few months as a parent, I felt really guilty about not seeing them enough after I moved out. Sometimes it could go weeks without even talking to them on the phone. I know it would totally break my heart if I didn't see my kids for that long. I have since really made an effort to see my parents at least once a week, and let them get as much quality time as possible with my whole family.

Edit: Spend as much time as you can with your parents, they most likely miss you more than you know, and they're not gonna be here forever.

Never quit.

Whenever my parents had a home repair project, they made me help them. When I was younger, this meant handing them the tool they asked for. As I got older, they made me more involved with the work. I still don't know if that is untrue, but now that I'm an adult I'm pretty sure it was just annoying for my mother to have me holding on to the stick shift all the time.

I have zero idea of the science and technical stuff behind it.

"It can be done". My dad always had a massive list of chores for us kids to do. We had an air conditioner in our garage that we were going to sell. My brother and I were told to move it from the garage down to the side of the road. We had a really long driveway so there was a large distance between the garage and the side of the road.

I was 11 at the time and my brother was 12. Window air conditioners are heavy and we couldn't do it. My dad used to be a body builder so we figured we would just go and tell him to do it since he was obviously strong enough. He yelled at us and was really mad. He said "you can't come inside until that air conditioner is sitting on the side of the road. I don't care if it takes you all day and night, I don't care if you are hungry, I don't care how you do it. The next time you come talk to me, it better be to tell me that the task is completed".

It weird because it seems like we were thinking we had to carry it down there. The reality is, we didn't think to put it in a little red wagon and pull it to the side of the road until he said he didn't care how we did it.

We had it done in no time but it is a memory I'll never forget. When I think I can do something, I look for a different way to do it. I also remove the time aspect from things. Timing is important but it isn't everything. Sometimes it's good just to finish. I'm not advocating a participation ribbon, just that it's a good self esteem booster.
Mother always said to me "don't do anything you would be ashamed of if found out later".
